meta.note: Values below are representative handbook/typical-batch figures (comparable to MMPDS, MatWeb, and standard aerospace materials references), not a specific mill certification. Real properties vary by heat treatment, batch, test temperature, and manufacturer -- verify against a datasheet before citing an exact number to a HAL panel. All values room-temperature unless otherwise noted.

items.garun_relevance: The most likely wing-spar material for a composite-skin/metal-spar hybrid layout, or as the comparison baseline if your team argues for a full-composite spar instead (§5.9 weight budget discussion).
items.description: The highest-strength common aerospace aluminum alloy, but with lower fracture toughness and corrosion resistance than 2024 -- typically used where strength matters more than damage tolerance.

items.garun_relevance: Standard fuselage-skin comparison point if the panel questions why your conceptual layout (§11.3) doesn't quantify skin material choice.
items.description: Lower strength than 7075 but significantly better fatigue and fracture-toughness performance -- the classic choice for fatigue-critical skin panels.

items.garun_relevance: The most realistic material for your battery pack's outer casing/frame (the SimScale thermal model's structural context) -- weldable, decent thermal conductivity, moderate strength, low cost relative to 7075.
items.description: Lower strength than 2024/7075 but weldable (unlike most high-strength aerospace aluminums) and easy to machine -- the default 'general purpose structural aluminum' choice.

typical_aerospace_applications: Weight-critical tankage/structure (e.g. Space Shuttle external tank)
items.garun_relevance: Worth naming if a reviewer challenges your 47.8% payload fraction (§5.9) and asks what advanced materials could plausibly support such a light airframe -- Al-Li alloys are a real, if costly, lever for weight reduction beyond standard 2024/7075.
items.description: Lithium addition reduces density (~3% lighter than conventional aluminum) while increasing stiffness -- historically justified only where weight savings are worth the higher material and processing cost.
